## Motivation {#sec-motivation}

Cabin lighting is an important part of the passenger experience in modern aircraft.
LED lamps allow an airline to change the colour and the brightness of the light for
different phases of a flight, such as boarding, cruise and night.
<!-- TODO cite: source on LED cabin lighting / light scenes -->

A cabin contains many lamp segments. Each segment needs precise and flicker-free
dimming, and all segments must follow the commands of one central controller.
At the same time, electronics for aircraft must be reliable, light and cost-effective.

Today, such lamps often use a dedicated multi-channel LED driver IC on each node.
A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) offers a different path. The same chip can
receive the communication protocol, generate the dimming signals and be changed later
by reprogramming. A modular digital design written for an FPGA can also be moved to an
application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) in the future.

This thesis explores that path in cooperation with AES Aircraft Elektro/Elektronik
System GmbH in Bremen. It uses the Cologne Chip GateMate FPGA and a fully open-source
toolchain (Yosys, nextpnr and openFPGALoader).
<!-- TODO cite: GateMate datasheet, Yosys, nextpnr, openFPGALoader -->

## Problem Statement {#sec-problem-statement}

The lighting system is a chain of lamp nodes. One master sends the data, and every
node passes the data on to the next node (daisy chain). In the AES system, the master
is a PIC microcontroller, and the protocol is the company's Flexlink protocol.

Each node in the chain must do four tasks:

1. take the data that belongs to its own LED segment,
2. forward the rest of the data to the next node without adding much delay,
3. convert its brightness values into accurate pulse-width modulation (PWM) signals
   for the LEDs, and
4. send answers, such as its address and temperature, back to the master.

@fig-system-architecture shows the system built in this work. A PC takes the role
of the master and sends Flexlink packets through a USB-to-serial adapter to the first
GateMate (GM1). GM1 keeps its own data and forwards the rest to the second GateMate
(GM2). The answers of both nodes travel back to the PC on a separate line.

![System architecture of the prototype: PC master, USB-TTL adapter and two daisy-chained GateMate nodes. Blue = uplink (master to segments), red = downlink (segments to master), green = PWM to the LED segment.](images/ch1_system_architecture){#fig-system-architecture width=100%}

The central question of this thesis is therefore:

> Can a small FPGA such as the Cologne Chip GateMate perform all four tasks of a lamp
> node, and can a chain of such nodes meet the requirements of an aircraft cabin
> lighting system?

## Objectives and Research Questions {#sec-objectives}

The main objective of this thesis is to design, prototype and evaluate an FPGA-based
digital control node for an aircraft cabin LED lamp. The work is guided by three
research questions:

- **RQ1:** Can one GateMate FPGA receive, decode and forward Flexlink data and at the
  same time drive the PWM channels of an RGBW LED segment?
- **RQ2:** Can a daisy chain of such nodes update the 25th segment within the required
  25 ms?
- **RQ3:** Which of the system requirements can the FPGA-based approach meet, and which
  can it not meet?

The requirements come from the AES concept brief and the digital aspect definition.
@tbl-key-requirements lists the most important ones. The full list follows in
Chapter 3.
<!-- TODO: change "Chapter 3" to @sec-requirements once that chapter has its label -->

| Requirement            | Target                                                  |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| LED channels           | 4 or more (R, G, B, W per segment)                      |
| Brightness resolution  | 16 bit per channel                                      |
| PWM type and frequency | Low-side PWM, above 400 Hz                              |
| Topology               | Daisy-chainable nodes                                   |
| Update time            | 25th segment in the chain updated within 25 ms          |
| Communication          | Flexlink: 1 MBaud, 9-bit words, SOP / data / EOP        |

: Key system requirements from AES {#tbl-key-requirements}

These requirements describe the whole lamp system (FPGA, driver stage and LEDs), not
only the FPGA. For this reason, the thesis states for each requirement whether it is
met, partly met or not achievable within the prototype.

From the main objective, the following goals are derived:

- a system-level model of the digital control in MATLAB/Simulink,
- modular, synthesizable Verilog code that can later be moved to an ASIC,
- Flexlink receive, forward and answer logic, with the same code on every node,
- automatic addressing of the nodes (Count Segments) and a downlink for answers,
- hardware validation on two GateMate evaluation boards.

## Scope, Limitations and Contributions {#sec-scope}

The focus of this thesis is the digital side: the Flexlink communication and the
forwarding logic in the FPGA. The power electronics come second.

**In scope:**

- PWM generation in the FPGA (four channels with 16 bit per node),
- the Flexlink uplink and downlink with cut-through forwarding,
- automatic addressing (Count Segments) and answer messages,
- a daisy-chain test with two nodes (PC → GM1 → GM2).

**Simplifications:**

- A PC with a USB-to-serial adapter acts as the Flexlink master instead of the PIC.
- The LED current is set by a series resistor per channel.
- The temperature value is a fixed placeholder (40 °C), because the sensor is not
  yet chosen.

**Not in scope:**

- a full chain of 25 segments in hardware (it is evaluated by calculation instead),
- certification for flight.
- [Confirm with professor: the "Black Box" — DC-DC converter, voltage level shifter
  and current-setting potentiometers.]

The main contributions of this thesis are:

1. a working Flexlink node on the GateMate FPGA, with the same design on every node,
2. cut-through forwarding with a delay of about 10.5 bit times per node,
3. automatic segment addressing with safety checks for wrong packets,
4. a complete open-source design flow from Verilog to a programmed FPGA.

## Methodology {#sec-methodology}

The work follows the V-model. On the left side of the V, the design moves from the
requirements down to the single modules. On the right side, each level is tested
against the matching level on the left.

<!-- TODO figure: V-model of this thesis (requirements <-> evaluation,
     architecture <-> hardware test, modules <-> simulation) -->

The work is organised in four overlapping phases:

1. **Requirements and system modelling:** collecting the requirements from AES and
   building a Simulink model of the data path (shift register, latch, 16-bit parsing
   and PWM generation).
2. **RTL design:** writing synthesizable Verilog for the Flexlink receiver,
   transmitter, forwarding logic, addressing and PWM.
3. **FPGA implementation and hardware validation:** synthesis with Yosys, place and
   route with nextpnr, programming with openFPGALoader, and tests on the GateMate
   boards with an oscilloscope.
4. **Evaluation and documentation:** checking each requirement and writing up the
   results.

## Structure of the Thesis {#sec-structure}

<!-- TODO: replace "Chapter X" with @sec-labels when the chapter files exist -->

Chapter 2 explains the background: LED dimming with PWM, FPGAs, the digital design
flow, serial communication and the Flexlink protocol.
Chapter 3 lists the requirements, analyses them and presents the system concept.
Chapter 4 describes the Simulink model of the data path.
Chapter 5 explains the Verilog design of the Flexlink node, module by module.
Chapter 6 covers the hardware setup and the tests on the GateMate boards.
Chapter 7 evaluates the results against the requirements and answers the research
questions.
Chapter 8 summarises the work and gives an outlook.
